ox: Wrong. Voltage-gated Na+ channels are not what changes in the photoreceptor. Light makes the rod hyperpolarize, so Na+ entry must fall, not rise. Trap: thinking depolarization machinery runs the light response.
Correct. Light activates rhodopsin, then transducin, then phosphodiesterase (PDE). PDE destroys cGMP, so cGMP-gated Na+ channels close and the rod hyperpolarizes.
Wrong. Glutamate release goes down in light, not up. Trap: mixing up the effect (less glutamate) with the cause (channel closure).
Wrong. Light converts 11-cis-retinal to all-trans-retinal, the reverse of this option. Trap: that step starts the cascade; it is not the direct cause of the hyperpolarization.

p: In darkness, a rod has a lot of cGMP (a small signaling molecule). cGMP holds Na+ channels open, so Na+ flows in and the cell stays partly depolarized (less negative). This is the dark current. The rod releases glutamate (a neurotransmitter) steadily.

Light changes retinal inside rhodopsin. Rhodopsin turns on transducin, which turns on phosphodiesterase. This enzyme breaks down cGMP. Channels close, Na+ stops entering, the cell hyperpolarizes, and glutamate release drops.

Light: rhodopsin, transducin, PDE, cGMP falls, channels close, hyperpolarization
Light causes hyperpolarization in photoreceptors
x6A_023.trap: Students assume light must depolarize a cell. In photoreceptors, light shuts a current off.

ox: Wrong. This describes OFF bipolar cells, which use glutamate-activated ionotropic receptors. Trap: forgetting that ON cells have the opposite receptor type.
Wrong. Bipolar cells make graded potentials and pass signals to ganglion cells. Ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve toward the thalamus.
Correct. ON bipolar cells have mGluR6 receptors, and glutamate hyperpolarizes them. In light, glutamate falls, so they depolarize.
Wrong. Bipolar cells are the direct targets of photoreceptor glutamate. Trap: skipping a layer of the retina.

p: Photoreceptors release glutamate in the dark and less in light. Bipolar cells are the next cell in the retina and split into two types that respond in opposite ways to the same glutamate.

ON bipolar cells have mGluR6 receptors. Glutamate on this receptor closes channels, so glutamate inhibits the cell. Less glutamate (light) means the cell depolarizes. OFF bipolar cells have receptors that glutamate excites, so light hyperpolarizes them.

ox: Wrong. Blindness in one eye comes from a lesion of one optic nerve before the chiasm. A chiasm lesion hits fibers from both eyes.

Correct. Fibers crossing at the chiasm come from the nasal retinas. Nasal retina sees the temporal (outer) field because the lens flips the image. So both temporal fields are lost (bitemporal hemianopia).
Wrong. Loss of the same side of the field in both eyes (homonymous) comes from a lesion behind the chiasm, such as the optic tract.
Wrong. Nasal field is seen by temporal retina, whose fibers stay on the same side and are not crossed here. Trap: forgetting the image flip.

p: The chiasm is where the two optic nerves meet. Only fibers from the nasal (inner, near the nose) half of each retina cross to the other side. Temporal (outer) retina fibers stay on the same side.

The lens flips the image, so nasal retina sees the outer (temporal) visual field. Cutting the crossing fibers removes the outer field of both eyes, like wearing horse blinders. Pituitary tumors commonly press here.

p: After the chiasm, each optic tract has fibers from both eyes. The left tract has the left eye's temporal retina and the right eye's nasal retina. Both of these retinal areas see the right side of the world.
